items.question: How do you assess the difference in energy use between generative models and models specifically trained for extractive question answering?
items.object: Energy use of generative models versus extractive question-answering models
items.answer: What we found is that for a given task, so for example, answering a question, something like, “What year was Napoleon born?” and you have a model that's specifically trained to extract information from text, so extractive question answering, versus a model that's a generative model that can also do the same kind of task but in a generative way, not creating new content way, the difference in terms of energy use is staggering. It's up to 30 times more for a generative type model.

It's up to 30 times more for a generative type model.

rubrics.text: The response states that a generative model can use up to 30 times as much energy as a model specifically trained for extractive question answering to perform the same question-answering task.

items.question: What made Hugging Face feel like the right research environment for you?
items.object: Hugging Face as a research workplace
items.answer: I was looking for a place where I could do the research I wanted to do in a positive environment where I get support. Essentially, I have issues with people telling me what to do. I mean, tried it, didn't like it. The whole rigid corporate structure wasn't for me, so I was like, maybe startups could be my thing. Except a lot of startups are really hectic and stressful, and then Hugging Face, I actually started part-time and I saw how people were actually pretty chill and really interested in responsible machine learning stuff like that. So I've been here for almost three years now.

items.question: How do you see the rise of generative AI affecting machine learning's contribution to fighting climate change?
items.object: The attention and climate impact of generative AI compared with non-generative climate applications
items.answer: What I've seen, I guess what's interesting is that there's a lot of climate-positive work going on. It's not getting a lot of attention. I'm still involved with Climate Change AI. It's grown a lot, and we still do workshops, summer schools, and all sorts of events. What's sad is that compared to GPT-type models, LLMs, the kind of OG climate work doesn't get as much interest nowadays because most of it actually uses non-generative methods. People are still into CNNs, people are still into random forests, and it actually is truly useful and impactful and can be applied in all these different contexts. And yet what we see is that people are trying to train the new climate GPT or whatever people call it nowadays. So I think that the work that I'm doing in trying to estimate the environmental impacts of these models is more and more relevant as they get deployed in society. But we do have this kind of catch-22: the models that are maybe the least useful so far in the fight against climate change also have a disproportionate climate impact, and vice versa, the most useful models are pretty lightweight. So it's pretty confusing.

items.question: How do you think public understanding of the environmental impacts of large language models has developed?
items.object: Public understanding of the environmental impacts of large language models
items.answer: I don't think that it's one of the early critiques. It has been raised, definitely, but I feel that it's kind of been dismissed a lot. The stochastic parrot paper, for example, there was—but I wouldn't say it's mainstream. I feel like every time I bring it up, people often talk about bias, they'll talk about hallucinations, for example, but when you start talking about the environmental impacts, I often get a blank stare, especially outside of the AI community. People are really like, “Oh, because people think it's the cloud.” Even often people will think that GPT or Midjourney or whatever is actually running on their phones and not on data centers, and they're like, “Well, if it's running on my phone, how bad can it be?” So I feel that broadly speaking, it hasn't really connected in people's minds that these things do have pretty disproportionate energy requirements compared to your average piece of software.

items.question: How do you make sense of the energy-use difference between generative models and models trained specifically for extractive question answering?
items.object: Energy use of generative versus extractive question-answering models
items.answer: We looked at a lot of open-source AI models from the Hugging Face platform, where people share these models, train and share these models. What we found is that for a given task, so for example, answering a question, “What year was Napoleon born?” and you have a model that's specifically trained to extract information from text, so extractive question answering, versus a model that's a generative model that can also do the same kind of task but in a generative way, not creating new content way, the difference in terms of energy use is staggering. It's up to 30 times more for a generative type model, which kind of makes sense because, on the one hand, my very first job was working on information retrieval and question answering. You're extracting existing content based on some measure of similarity, some kind of vector arithmetic or hashing. It's relatively straightforward in terms of computation. We used to be using Elasticsearch and stuff like that in my first job. But for generative approaches, you've got usually a pretty big model, and that has to actually take the query and add to it, generate new content. From an intuitive perspective, it does make sense that it uses a lot more energy.

items.question: Why did you focus your study of AI energy use on deployment?
items.object: The energy cost of deploying AI models
items.answer:
Our goal was really to look at AI deployment. Most of the papers to date were looking at the training step, which is a little bit easier to get a handle on because it's like you press start, you train your model for, I don't know, three million hours, and then you press stop and calculate how much energy you used. But deployment is a little bit more tricky because most models, if they're in production, are constantly on and constantly replying to queries. Oftentimes you've got multiple copies of the model running depending on the load, and you've got all sorts of things, so people tended not to look at deployment because it was kind of messy.

What we did is we took a bunch of models, like 90 models from the Hugging Face Hub, and measured how much energy they were using for the same set of tasks, of queries. We looked at image generation, text generation, text classification, image captioning, a lot of different tasks. The idea was to see how tasks compared, how models compared, and identify some trends with regards to deploying AI models in practice. We also looked at model size. For example, we looked at text generation models of different sizes and the trade-off between how much energy was used for training the model and for each model query. Depending on the size of the model, it varied between, I think, 50 million to 200 million queries to have the equivalent energy of a training run, which may seem like a lot. On the other hand, if you have a production-level system like ChatGPT that gets millions of queries a day, within a couple of weeks you've used as much energy for deploying the model as you did for training it.

We also looked at image generation, and the climate cost of inference in the long term is much larger than the training cost, at least for models that eventually make their way into production. Models that don't make their way into production is an entirely different question.

items.question: How do you assess whether the trend toward smaller, more efficient AI models represents progress on energy use?
items.object: The trend toward offering smaller, more efficient AI models alongside larger models
items.answer: It's hard to say because there's honestly very little transparency. It's true that before, people would almost be like, “We trained a bigger and bigger model just so we can say that it's the biggest model.” So there was 160 billion, 170 billion, 100 billion, and nowadays you do often see people train bigger models and then concurrently say, “And we have a smaller, more efficient model.” So it's not quite a win, but I do see that there's reflection.

items.question: How do you see Hugging Face’s role in addressing both climate impact and the concentration of power in AI?
items.object: Hugging Face, model reuse, and the concentration of power in AI
items.answer: I definitely chose Hugging Face as a place of employment, not only from a climate perspective, because I do see that having a hub where people can find models easily does, in an indirect way, kind of work like recycling. I'm not going to train my own model; maybe I'm going to start with a base model and fine-tune it. It helps people reuse models. I also believe that monopoly or concentration of power isn't a very healthy dynamic for any industry. I did see, and still do see to some extent, a concentration of power in AI. Meredith Whittaker talks about this a lot. These bigger and bigger models really do put bigger companies at an advantage in terms of who has the resources to run them, train them, deploy them. So I believe there's a climate perspective, but there's also the democratization perspective that Hugging Face fits well into. If we want more innovation, more startups, nonprofits, and academia having more accessible models is important. Students starting a PhD can't afford to run an 80-billion-parameter model, but maybe they want to do a project or a hackathon. To enable them to do that, we need open-source, smaller open-source models. I see it as an advantage on different levels, one of which is climate.

items.object: Smaller AI models as a connection between sustainability and equity
items.answer: Something I was working on recently, a paper with folks from the Data & Society Institute, is about how in the context of AI ethics, sustainability and climate are really related. Maybe a smaller model will have less climate impact, but it will also be more accessible in terms of justice and equity in our field. We had a lot of conversations about how helping people access or train smaller models can have impacts that go above and beyond simple energy or the environment. items.question: What did you find interesting about studying BLOOM's carbon footprint?
items.object: The study of BLOOM's carbon footprint
items.answer: I was part of the working group that aimed to measure BLOOM's carbon footprint. It was interesting because we were using French compute that was relatively low carbon, but also we did a really in-depth study of the training logs. We could go really deep into what each part of the process was in terms of training smaller models, experimentation, all those different little pieces of the puzzle, how they fit together.

items.question: How do you think transparency in AI research has changed over the past few years?
items.object: Transparency in AI research and scientific conferences
items.answer: I agree that Llama is still accessible, but if you look at a couple of years ago, I still feel that the field of AI has become less transparent. If you look at conferences, three or four years ago, if you submitted a paper to a conference, you had to give a certain amount of information about how big the model was, where the data was coming from, things like that. Nowadays, I feel like you could submit a model that's behind a paywall and just give some examples of how great the images are, how convincing the video is, and that's kind of okay as well, even though it's a scientific conference.

items.question: Why do you find current AI evaluation unreliable for deciding which language model is better?
items.object: Evaluation and comparison of language models
items.answer: I find that evaluation in AI has become so broken. I know people are doing stuff, but when you start digging into the details, usually when you're evaluating a language model it's by prompting. People use different prompt approaches, or sometimes they'll sample, top five, top K, and then compare it with a fine-tuned model that has a set, a limited number of options, of categories or labels it can choose from. Sometimes the comparisons are apples to oranges, and it's really hard to even say. Often language models aren't replicable. They do some evaluation, then you do it again and can't get the same result. I found that evaluation is just so hard to say which model is better. People keep inventing new benchmarks and finding that the benchmarks are in the training data. Every time I read something, I have so many questions that aren't really answered.

items.question: How do you view the research community's shift from fine-tuned models toward general-purpose language models?
items.object: The research shift from fine-tuned models to general-purpose language models
items.answer: Theoretically, general-purpose or multitask models are supposed to be better than fine-tuned models, but people have kind of given up on working on fine-tuned models. Recently I wrote a position paper accepted to ICML with a colleague of mine, A. Rogers from Copenhagen, and we wanted to look at tasks where people were still working on tuned models and multitask models. We couldn't find many, because people are all gung-ho about large language models and tend to work on these general tasks, general language understanding and things like that. We had a lot of trouble trying to find concrete evidence for the fact that the evaluation doesn't make much sense.

items.question: Why are you skeptical of claims of breakthroughs in AI model capabilities?
items.object: Claims of emergent capabilities and state-of-the-art performance in AI models
items.answer: I think that we're also cherry-picking a lot of results. For example, the concept of emergent properties is something we talk about in our position paper. When you talk about emergent properties, you assume that things almost magically appear, and you're like, “Oh, this model just magically is able to do this thing that it wasn't trained for.” But we don't know exactly what goes into the training data, and this data is so big. For example, GPT whatever passed the law exam, the bar exam, but maybe all the books are in there. We don't know. There are all these issues with the claims that people make. Same with state of the art: often it's a new data set—or a new task, like drawing a unicorn.

items.question: Why do you see replicability as essential to progress in machine learning research?
items.object: Replicability in machine learning research
items.answer: I'm a little bit skeptical because I miss the good old days where you could replicate or check or reproduce people's work. Nowadays, I feel there's the access issue of models that are just behind an API, so you can't look at what's under the hood, but it's also the fact that you can't reproduce results. That's so frustrating from a scientific perspective because for me it's the basic thing: if you make a claim, I should be able to replicate that claim. That's how science works, that we keep building on each other's experiments or discoveries. Whereas in machine learning, I feel a lot of the discoveries, innovations, or claims are missing this core element of replicability. If I can't even replicate what you've done, how can I continue building upon it?

Nowadays, I feel there's the access issue of models that are just behind an API, so you can't look at what's under the hood, but it's also the fact that you can't reproduce results. That's so frustrating from a scientific perspective because for me it's the basic thing: if you make a claim, I should be able to replicate that claim. That's how science works, that we keep building on each other's experiments or discoveries. Whereas in machine learning, I feel a lot of the discoveries, innovations, or claims are missing this core element of replicability. If I can't even replicate what you've done, how can I continue building upon it?

items.question: Why do you find machine learning results difficult to reproduce even when researchers have access to the models?
items.object: Reproducibility of machine learning research
items.answer:
It's access. It's also often that some element is missing, either the data or sometimes the actual evaluation approach. There's great work out of EleutherAI, who created an evaluation harness, because they found that a lot of the times every time someone would train a new LLM, they would do their own thing in terms of evaluation, and so things weren't necessarily apples to apples. There's that as well, the actual procedure used.

Language models are stochastic, they're unpredictable, and often people won't fix the random seed or report it. I can't reproduce the results you report, even if I have access to the model, the training data, and the code, because some random seed is missing. I was helping organize the ML Reproducibility Challenge a couple of years ago. People can choose a paper accepted to one of the core ML conferences and try to replicate the results. An overwhelming majority of the time, people weren't able to because there was always some little detail missing. They had to correspond with the authors, reverse engineer a bunch of things, and year in, year out, it would be that the majority of ML research is not reproducible.

items.question: How do you assess the reporting requirements in the NeurIPS code of ethics you helped develop?
items.object: NeurIPS code of ethics and its reporting requirements
items.answer: I helped develop the code of ethics. There was replicability, climate impact, accessibility. Technically, you were supposed to say how much you paid crowdsourced workers if you had any, et cetera. That's kind of the gold standard, but in practice there's always this tension between how much you can do, or how much you even save this information. Sometimes people don't even bother counting how many GPU hours they used. A lot of the pushback we got when we introduced this code of ethics at NeurIPS in 2023 was that it was asking too much from people.

items.question: How do you think Energy Star's approach to appliance ratings should inform energy-efficiency ratings for AI models?
items.object: Applying the Energy Star approach to AI model efficiency ratings
items.answer:
I was really inspired by that work because you're not forcing people to take this into account, but typically people do care about their energy usage at home, and they increasingly care about environmental impacts as well. The idea is to harness the same kind of measurement where you compare for a given task. For a washing machine category, you compare different models. What's interesting is that the EPA doesn't really measure performance. They're not going to look at how well the washer washes socks or whatever. Given a standard load, the default setting, they'll measure energy consumption, which I find interesting because they're two different things. Performance can depend on how you're using the appliance and how you're using the AI model. Maybe some people really need it to be top state of the art, but other people just wash their laundry and it doesn't have to completely take out all the stains from your white shirts.

I spoke to the folks from the EPA, and they're like, “Well, performance is a secondary thing. The people who make the appliances can measure that as they will depending on different types of loads, but we measure efficiency for a default setting.” I'm taking a similar approach for the AI Energy Star project. I identified 10 different tasks, everything from text generation, image generation, image captioning, speech recognition, all sorts of tasks across modalities. For each task, I'm comparing models from the Hugging Face Hub that can do that task. I'm not benchmarking them in terms of whatever benchmark, but really in terms of energy efficiency. The idea is to create a range for each task, and then once you have that range from minimum to maximum, you can start giving categories.

items.question: Why do you think AI model providers and users will engage with a voluntary Energy Star rating system for models?
items.object: Voluntary participation in Energy Star ratings for AI models
items.answer: I'm going to start with open-source models, and I'm already talking to, for example, Cohere, Meta, Microsoft. I've reached out to all of them, and I'm going to provide a script, a Docker, essentially, that they can run locally and they don't need to give up any state company secrets. It's really a standardized kind of script that all the models can be compared with, and hopefully everybody will be incentivized to participate. Big tech companies do care about efficiency, compute, and showing that it's the same as for appliances. You want your appliance to have an Energy Star rating that's considered cool, good for the planet or green. I'm hoping to have something similar for AI. Maybe I'm a little bit naive, but I believe most people in our community care about efficiency and compute. The structures are not in place yet for them to take this into account when sharing or choosing models. Given the right information, people can use this to make more informed decisions.

items.question: How do you approach measuring energy use for your proposed AI model ratings?
items.object: Measuring energy use for AI model ratings
items.answer: I'm counting energy usage for a specific GPU model. The idea is to run your model on this GPU. I helped create a package called CodeCarbon way back when, and it's grown and thrived. It's a Python package, a Python library that measures energy consumption of different pieces of hardware—GPU, CPU, RAM—and also, depending on where the energy is coming from, depending on how it's generated, estimates carbon emissions. I'm using CodeCarbon in the project in order to have that amount of energy.

items.question: Why do you think AI model benchmarks should distinguish models by the hardware they need to run?
items.object: Grouping AI models by hardware requirements for benchmarking
items.answer: We'll compare something that can run locally on a small GPU that only has a couple of gigs of memory versus something that needs a commercial 24-, 48-gig GPU versus one that needs multiple, because I feel that it's not quite the same use case. To go with the metaphor of washing machines, you have smaller ones. In Europe they often have these tiny washing machines; we tend to have a little bit bigger ones, and then there are more commercial-level washing machines that you'll use for washing, I don't know, parachutes or whatnot.

items.question: How do you think AI energy-efficiency leaderboards should account for different tasks and modalities?
items.object: Comparing AI models’ energy efficiency across tasks and modalities
items.answer: There's an LM-per-watt leaderboard on Hugging Face, but it's mostly only LLMs. It doesn't look at object detection or speech recognition or whatever. Given the diversity of tasks that exist in AI, it's good to consider all different modalities. This is something we found in the “Watts the Cost” paper: tasks with images, either image captioning or image generation, are orders of magnitude more energy-intensive than tasks that only have text. Comparing the two is difficult, and increasingly as models are getting multimodal, it's important to reflect that and compare apples with apples: compare multimodal models with multimodal models, and not text generation models, because it's a completely different ball game.

items.question: Why do you favor task-specific or context-specific AI models for real-world applications?
items.object: Task-specific or context-specific AI models
items.answer: This goes back to what you want to do with the model. Maybe in research we optimize the multitask nature of LLMs or AI models generally, and I feel that is something that we really pursue. But in other applications, in the real world, maybe you don't need models that are so complex. In my very first job, we were working with IBM Watson, and we had an intent classifier upstream in the model. Depending on what the intent was, a different model would be activated. It wouldn't always be the whole kit and caboodle that was activated; the query didn't go through all the models at once. I feel we've maybe come back to this with mixture of experts, but for a while there we expected models to do everything. I feel that's unrealistic. You can't be good at everything. I don't think AI models can be good at all possible tasks. I'm a big fan of task-specific models, or at least context-specific models.

items.question: Why do you think comparing energy efficiency across very different AI tasks is misleading?
items.object: Comparing energy efficiency across AI tasks in the “Watts the Cost” study
items.answer: The idea was to represent common tasks. On Hugging Face we have these task pipelines, common task pipelines that people use. In the “Watts the Cost” study, we saw it doesn't make sense to compare very different tasks. Sentiment analysis, text classification, is so lightweight; it makes no sense to compare that with image generation, which is on the other end of the spectrum in terms of energy efficiency.

items.question: How do you think about the trade-off when comparing the energy use of multitask and single-task AI models?
items.object: Energy comparisons between multitask and single-task AI models
items.answer: Often, for example, you have to prompt the T5. You have to say, “What's the answer to this question, and here's the context,” so you always also add some input that will make comparisons difficult. People brought this up when we wrote “Watts the Cost,” and it's true that it is hard to compare multitask and single-task models. But if people are using them for all sorts of things, it's good to see: maybe if it does 30 different tasks but it's 30 times more energy, maybe it's okay at the end of the day. It's a trade-off of what you're comfortable with and how you're using the model.

items.question: Why do you find it difficult to compare fine-tuned models with multitask models on a task like sentiment classification?
items.object: Comparing fine-tuned models with multitask models
items.answer: I also have the prompt that I have to say, “Categorize—I don't know, whatever, give the sentiment of the following sentence.” So the input is going to be longer. And when you think about it, in one case you just have the two categories to choose from, the two labels, and on the other hand you have all of the vocab for the model to choose from. Sometimes it doesn't even say positive or negative; sometimes it says red, and you're like, “Well, how?” Or something more complex, like, “Oh, this is actually a very nuanced...” If I want to compare fine-tuned with multitask models, I quickly see that it's really hard to compare the two.

items.question: What have you learned from AI model documentation efforts about making your AI energy-rating process easy for people to adopt?
items.object: Lessons from AI model documentation for adoption of an AI energy-rating process
items.answer:
I think that model cards have become pretty much a standard. At Hugging Face, I think the vast majority of models will—I mean, probably not the full model card with all of the information, but they'll have a subset of information that's shared. I guess what I learned is that people won't want to spend hours on this kind of stuff. It's hard to incentivize people to document their work. This is why I want it to be a simple script that someone can run, or if they don't have the in-house compute, a simple query or button they can press that I'll run for them, or whatever. I'll set up a process to run it for them. I want to make this as seamless as possible because what I've seen is as soon as documenting data or documenting models becomes a bit more complex, people run out of patience. It's hard to keep the enthusiasm alive.

On the other hand, I've seen some really great efforts recently of being thorough and systematic. For example, Allen Institute recently trained their model OLMo, and they did a great job of really doing amazing, in-depth documentation of the data and the model.
